cells.tense: You are at the threshold right now, and this practice is already arriving through it.
cells.act: stand in the gap it leaves without rebuilding yet
cells.ask: When something you kept up stops fitting, stand there a moment with the space open. Don't start refilling it. Just notice what the open space is like before the next thing comes.
cells.core:
The slow work is entering your life and meeting no resistance. You show up, you repeat something small, and the repetition gives back more than it costs. The solitude is not a wall you're behind — it's where the work gets done, and people who matter to you can feel it rather than resent it. Refinement is for you, not against you; you are not measuring yourself against a standard that keeps moving.

Something you've been holding up is going to come down, and it won't need your help to fall. When that moment comes, the pull will be to shore it up fast or replace it with something better. Let it lie a week, and keep your ordinary practice going through it. The clearing is the point; it isn't the start of a new problem. What you keep up will stand without your arms around it.
cells.sheetLine: The work is arriving and it doesn't need forcing.
cells.verb: keep a small light lit through plain repetition
cells.place: the doorstep where what's arriving comes in

cells.tense: You are pushing ahead into a version of this practice that hasn't arrived yet.
cells.act: put it down and leave your hands empty a while
cells.ask: Pick the piece you're gripping hardest — a standard, a streak, a way it has to look — and set it down. Leave your hands empty. Practise anyway, plain and a little worse, until the grip releases in its own time.
cells.core:
The practice has gotten tighter, not deeper. Somewhere the repetition turned into a standard to match, and the matching now takes as much energy as the work itself. Solitude starts to feel required rather than chosen; stepping away feels like a loss you can't afford. You get sharper, and the point recedes. That's the sign it has crossed; the light isn't reaching the work anymore.

What's coming in behind this will land better if your hands are free. Put one thing down on purpose, while you still know exactly where it sits — not because you failed at it, but because you finished what it was for. Then the empty hour isn't a hole. Let nothing fill it, and see what the practice looks like when you're no longer holding it upright.
cells.sheetLine: The grip on the practice is the thing wearing you out.
cells.verb: keep a small light lit through plain repetition
cells.place: the doorstep where what's arriving comes in

cells.tense: You kept at this once, and the way back in still feels blocked behind you.
cells.act: let an exchange flow both ways
cells.ask: Do something for a person who didn't ask. When they offer something back, let it land — don't wave it off, don't match it. Keep letting exchanges run both directions over time and keep no tally of them.
cells.core:
The repetition sits in your past. Not abandoned, exactly — more like a door you stopped at and the body learned not to try again. You can watch other people build a skill over time and feel the distance from it, and no amount of wanting has closed that. Nothing here says what put the door there; the fact is enough: some of you is not showing up to the work, and the work hasn't asked you to.

What's arriving now comes in through exchange. Give something and let something come back, both ways, with the ledger closed. That reopens the channel that keeps a practice fed — you're not meant to run it on nothing. The one who takes as readily as they give is the one who can keep showing up. The door wasn't locked. It just hadn't been opened from both sides.
cells.sheetLine: You paused at the door and the work is still there.

cells.place: the doorstep where what's arriving comes in

cells.tense: You are practising right now and your account of it leaves that out.
cells.act: take the next step with only enough light for that step
cells.ask: Next time you're in the middle of something you've done a hundred times, move through it knowing your own hand is in the moving. No announcement, no explanation. Just keep going, hands on it, and see where the road shows itself.
cells.core:
There's a competence in your hands that you call something else — instinct, talent, just how things go. You've done the repetition, and the repetition is where the ease came from. Other people watching would say you worked at that. Your own story skips the part where you built it, so what you have looks like something you were given rather than something you made.

The next move doesn't require a full confession of the practice. Take one step and know your own hand in it — that's the whole difference between being carried and walking. You will not see the whole road, and you don't need to; you need only enough light for this step. After a few of those, the picture you sketch of your own life will have the maker in it. That's what there is to keep.
cells.sheetLine: This competence is yours. Your story skips where it came from.

attempts.check: The unsupported claims are "past experiences have made practice feel dangerous" (Too Little) and "you don't know you're practicing — or refusing to" (Unacknowledged); neither is entailed by the draw, so both cells locate the person's present position without naming any history, cause, or refusal. A reader could reasonably say the practice isn't dangerous, just pointless or eroded, and the Too Little cell is written so that objection still leaves something usable. The Too Much ask — let go of what you're gripping — survives being wrong because it asks for one grip released and builds nothing on it, and the four asks open on four verbs (stand, leave, trade, take), none needing money, time, or another person on hand. The sentence serving the writer rather than the person is any hint that the repetition has a hidden origin story; it's cut.
